# Cognitive research

In the subsection below, I cite passages from 

- "Weinstein, Y., Sumeracki, M. A., & Caviglioli, O. (2018). Teaching the
  science of learning. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implication"
  https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s41235-017-0087-y

  > "we focus on six specific cognitive strategies that have received robust support
  > from decades of research: spaced practice, interleaving, retrieval practice,
  > elaboration, concrete examples, and dual coding. "

Claude: (TODO: replace by real citations from the articles)

  > "**No retrieval, therefore weak retention.** The testing effect is one of
  > the most robust results in the field (Roediger and Karpicke, 2006):
  > retrieving information strengthens memory far more than re-studying it. A
  > frontal hour contains close to zero retrieval attempts by the student. The
  > material is encoded once, passively, and then decays. This is arguably the
  > single largest missed opportunity of the format, and also the cheapest to
  > fix.

  > "**Fluency creates an illusion of learning, for both parties.** A
  > well-delivered lecture is easy to follow, and ease of processing is misread
  > as mastery — Bjork's (1994) work on metacognitive illusions and desirable
  > difficulties. Students then report learning more from a polished lecture
  > than from a harder active format, *while actually learning less* on the
  > test: Deslauriers et al. (2019) randomly assigned students in introductory
  > physics to active and passive versions of the same content and found actual
  > learning and feeling of learning strongly anticorrelated. The lecturer,
  > seeing nodding faces, receives the same false signal. The format
  > systematically misinforms everyone about whether it is working.


## Spacing vs craming

Weinstein et al 2018

> It is important to note that students may feel less confident when they space
> their learning (Bjork, 1999) than when they cram. This is because spaced
> learning is harder – but it is this “desirable difficulty” that helps
> learning in the long term (Bjork, 1994).


### Desirable difficulties

Bjork 1994:

> "A trainer, in effect, is vulnerable to a type of operant conditioning, where
> the reinforcing events are improvements in the performance and/or happiness
> of trainees. Such a conditioning process, over time, can act to shift the
> trainer toward manipulations that increase the rate of correct responding —
> that make the trainee’s life easier, so to speak. Doing that, of course, will
> move the trainer away from introducing the types of desirable difficulties
> summarized in the preceding section. The tendency for instructors to be
> pushed toward training programs that maximize the performance or evaluative
> reaction of their trainees during is exacerbated by certain institutional
> characteristics that are common in real-world organizations. First, those
> responsible for training are often themselves evaluated in terms of the
> performance and satisfaction of their trainees during training, or at the
> end of training. Second,individuals with the day-to-day responsibility for
> training often do not get a chance to observe the post training performance of
> the people they have trained; a trainee’s later successes and failures tend
> to occur in settings that are far removed from the original training
> environment, and from the trainer himself or herself. It is also rarely the
> case that systematic measurements of post training on-the-job performance
> are even collected, let alone provided to a trainer as a guide to what
> manipulations do and do not achieve the post training goals of training. And,
> finally, where refresher or retraining programs exist, they are typically
> the concern of individuals other than those responsible for the original
> training."


## Retrieval vs restudy

Weinstein et al 2018:

> "The benefit of retrieval practice depends to a certain extent on successful
> retrieval (see Karpicke, Lehman, et al., 2014). For example, in Experiment 4
> of Smith et al. (2013), students successfully retrieved 72% of the
> information dur- ing retrieval practice. Of course, retrieving 72% of the
> information was compared to a restudy control group, during which students
> were re-exposed to 100% of the information, creating a bias in favor of the
> restudy condi- tion. Yet retrieval led to superior memory later compared to
> the restudy control. However, if retrieval success is extremely low, then it
> is unlikely to improve memory (e.g., Karpicke, Blunt, et al., 2014),
> particularly in the absence of feedback."

Weinstein et al 2018 on testing:

> "Retrieval practice has received a lot of attention in teacher blogs (see
> “Learning Scientists” (2016b) for a collection). A common theme seems to be
> an emphasis on low-stakes (Young, 2016) and even no-stakes (Cox, 2015)
> testing, the goal of which is to increase learning rather than assess
> performance"

## Definitions of learning

### Homography

-  Ilya Sutskever presents an Observation on Generalization  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AKMuA_TVz3A&t=4s

    > "Why would data have regularities that our machine learning models can
    > capture?"

    - Perplexity explaining an analogy between homography and the way transformers
      simulate alternative architecture internally 
      https://www.perplexity.ai/search/what-is-sgd-in-this-context-yo-rLzyIfSWRE27gHO4eut_WA#1

      > "Ilya Sutskever views deep neural networks, including transformers, as
      > universal parallel computers capable of universal computation given
      > enough scale. These models execute sequential operations (like
      > attention layers) in parallel across massive hardware, simulating
      > arbitrary programs during training via optimization like Stochastic
      > Gradient Descent (SGD). 

      > Homography refers to a projective transformation in computer vision and
      > geometry that maps points from one plane (or image) to another while
      > preserving lines and incidence relations, typically via a 3x3 matrix. It's
      > like a "micro" version because neural networks, especially transformers, can
      > efficiently simulate one architecture inside another through such
      > transformations, much as computers emulate each other.
  
      > The "micro homography" idea emphasizes robustness: just as a homography
      > seamlessly warps one planar view into another without losing structural
      > fidelity (e.g., in image stitching), transformers can "warp" or
      > simulate alternative architectures internally. This makes them
      > interchangeable in capability—depth vs. width, dense vs. sparse
      > attention—when optimization is strong, as minor changes are absorbed
      > like viewpoint shifts in projective geometry. Architectural tweaks
      > matter mainly for bottlenecks or efficiency, not core expressivity.


## AGI doesn't exist

- https://www.perplexity.ai/search/what-does-sergey-s-return-mean-jVvbrHr2T3Ck51YQu4jOSQ#2

    > "Yann LeCun, argues that AGI often defined as human-level or superhuman
    > intelligence across all domains is a flawed, overhyped concept because
    > intelligence is inherently relative and context-specific. Humans excel in
    > narrow, evolved skills like social reasoning, tool use, and survival in
    > physical environments, but lag in raw pattern recognition or data
    > processing compared to animals or machines; for instance, cats outperform
    > humans in visuomotor tasks."

    > "Why It Still Matters"

    > "LeCun's view doesn't negate practical AI progress; it reframes "AGI" as
    > unnecessary hype, emphasizing "human-level AI" for specific, valuable
    > capabilities like world modeling or robotics, where Google (under Brin's
    > push) and others compete. In the poster's context, Brin's return signals
    > Google's execution on these frontiers—Gemini advancements in multimodal
    > models—not chasing an ill-defined AGI finish line. Real-world dominance
    > in video/images (YouTube data) and chips (TPUs) drives usage wins,
    > regardless of terminology."
